content.comment_body: Hello colleagues, greetings from Costa Rica. I am trying to set up communication between several [product_name] [version_no] modules via Ethernet to automate my house and workshop. These devices have been resilient against lightning and rough conditions for over 14 years, and I believe they’ll outlast other PLCs I’ve used. However, I can’t find up-to-date manuals or guides on the [company_name] website, nor in the [product_name] software help files, for passing orders or I/O signals between units. Any suggestions on resources or advice would be appreciated. Responses in German or Spanish are welcome. [user_name] 10`N,84`W
Hi, You might want to bookmark this site: Application examples for [product_name]. [url] Regards,

Thank you so much, [user_name]. This link is much more helpful compared to what I've found so far, which was mostly vague information. I haven’t checked the sample projects yet, but the overview looks promising and seems to answer several questions. I was considering going back to my usual PLCs, but the fact that I have a box full of failed units to return to the factory—while only 3 or 4 [product_name] modules have failed in 14 years, and apparently not due to lightning—makes the choice clear. I use [product_name] modules for on-site emergencies and smaller automation projects, and only recently discovered there’s a forum for sharing support. I’d like to see more activity here like in other communities I frequent. Let’s see what the future brings. Best wishes from across the ocean. [user_name]
Are the servers always this slow? It took me nearly an hour just to find this thread! Wishing you a happy Advent season from Costa Rica. Hopefully something will work soon. [user_name]

For now, I’ve only been able to review some of the sample applications as the site was extremely slow—it brought back memories of dial-up connections in the early 2000s. Tomorrow is another day. Good evening. [user_name]

I first experimented with master/slave mode and was surprised to find that the slave’s existing program gets disabled in slave mode. The slave LB program reactivates when switching back to master mode, but then the master LA no longer receives signals from the slave. This could potentially be a workaround for certain communication problems we have during rainy seasons, but it’s not ideal to have to be onsite just to keep machines operating in ‘emergency mode,’ especially since our operators are not technically skilled. Is there a way to automate the Master-Slave switching when communication fails? Now I’m going to try master/master communication—I’m hoping a computer or HMI won’t be required. From initial reading, it seems a bit complicated due to the VW addresses. It’s always interesting to try new features of a trusted tool (and take a break from client requests for a bit). [user_name]

Hello [user_name], I’d like to share some additional information. You can explore recent application examples related to home automation using Ethernet communication with multiple [product_name] modules. [url] [url] [url] By reading these, you can choose whether Master-Slave or Server-Client communication best suits your needs. Both approaches can be used together as shown in the examples, which include complete code and step-by-step guides for download. Regards, [user_name]

[user_name], thanks for the links. Yesterday I had to hurry to customs where my motorcycle with a sidecar arrived and someone from the warehouse had taken all the spare parts out, claiming they weren’t part of the paperwork. So my agent had extra work due to a minor mistake. For me, at least, it was a nice early Christmas gift—it’s never too late to enjoy childhood! I hadn’t seen my bike for months. I’ll continue looking into new possibilities for [product_name] as soon as I’m back in the workshop. [user_name]
Hello [user_name], thank you for your feedback. If you have any further questions, feel free to ask. Regards, [user_name]

I finally figured out how to set up the cross-references needed for master-to-master operation using VB addresses. For any project, starting with the cross-reference list is essential, and as you start adding expansion modules, things can get complicated. From what I’m seeing, it makes me think it’s easier to stick with the PLCs I’ve used for years rather than dive into a technology that feels like stepping back a decade. There’s a saying here in Costa Rica: ‘Better the devil you know than the devil you don’t.’ For my work, the K&P nini DDCs I’m familiar with are definitely more flexible for scalable projects, though the [product_name] modules are easier to program. Anyway, I’ll move forward with this [product_name] setup since it’s affordable, robust, and readily available locally. My next challenge is figuring out how to integrate a Kinko touch panel into the [product_name] network. Once that’s done, I’ll have to carefully prepare a large cross-reference sheet before programming. Wishing you a happy Nikolaustag. [user_name]

analysis.insight_summary: An experienced user of [product_name] modules for smaller automation and home/workshop control is struggling to configure reliable Ethernet-based communication between multiple [product_name] [version_no] units. Key issues include outdated or inaccessible documentation, non-intuitive master/slave switching that deactivates slave functionality, and complex cross-referencing when expanding the system. While the user values the durability and low failure rates of [product_name], they find the solution less flexible and scalable than other PLC options. Positive points include robustness and availability, but communication setup is challenging and documentation is lacking.
analysis.user_expectations: The user expects accessible, up-to-date documentation with practical examples of Ethernet communication for multiple [product_name] modules, seamless program switching or robust fault tolerance, and easy integration with system expansions and third-party devices.
